<SUMMARY>The global geopolitical landscape for June 19-26, 2026, was dominated by intense competition in the semiconductor and critical minerals sectors, driven by the expanding demands of artificial intelligence (AI). The United States continued its efforts to secure supply chains and manufacturing capabilities, notably through the Pax Silica initiative and a cobalt deal with Congo, while pushing back on China's technological advancement. Europe expressed concerns over Washington's chip war and focused on internal chip sovereignty. China actively invested in its domestic semiconductor industry and tightened export controls on key minerals like indium, simultaneously showcasing AI applications at its supply chain expo. Military and space developments highlighted advancements in command and control systems and the national security risks posed by quantum computing. India positioned itself for significant semiconductor investments, while West Asia saw ongoing discussions regarding energy stability, AI adoption, and military engagements in Israel. These dynamics underscore a global race for technological supremacy and resource control, with significant implications for international trade, energy security, and defense postures.</SUMMARY>
<EWS>The reliance on Chinese-controlled critical minerals, such as indium, presents an ongoing supply chain vulnerability as China tightens export controls amid rising AI demand. The potential for the US MATCH Act to further restrict access to older-generation deep ultraviolet (DUV) tools for Chinese chipmakers could escalate tech tensions. Quantum computing poses serious national security risks, particularly in code-breaking, necessitating robust cybersecurity measures. India's rapid AI data center expansion is on a collision course with severe water scarcity in key technological hubs, threatening sustainable growth. The global deep ocean floor remains largely unmapped to modern standards, limiting knowledge of potential seabed resources that could become vital geopolitical leverage points. Furthermore, African nations face critical mineral exploitation and refinery bottlenecks, indicating a need for localized processing capabilities to avoid exporting raw resources without value addition.</EWS>
<EXEC>
**Asia:**
China's National Silicon Industry Group (NSIG), a leading 12-inch silicon wafer maker, announced a CNY11.45 billion (US$1.6 billion) capital injection into its core subsidiary Shanghai Xinsheng Semiconductor Technology, aiming to ease losses through restructuring. China's premier urged AI governance to avoid "losing control." The 4th China International Supply Chain Expo debuted an AI section, featuring participants like Nvidia, Intel, and Alibaba, to showcase AI applications in supply chain resilience. Alibaba sued the US Defense Department in a bid to remove its "Chinese military company" designation. China’s chipmaking supply chain runs through Southeast Asia. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) recorded monthly revenue for May 2026 at NT$416.98 billion, a 30.1% increase year-over-year. Taiwan is weighing AI chip export controls, and its AI supply chain boom is fueling investment and exports, with GDP growth topping a 10% outlook. Micron Technology expects early product shipments from its Taiwan fab site by mid-2027. South Korea's IPO activity has lagged behind regional peers due to its market structure and governance reforms. Japan experienced worsening difficulties in procuring naphtha and other oil products for nearly 70% of surveyed firms in May.

**Europe:**
Dutch Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma visited Washington to oppose the MATCH Act, a proposed bill to bar Chinese chipmakers from accessing Western semiconductor equipment. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet noted that China can currently purchase older-generation deep ultraviolet tools, which the MATCH Act would restrict. The Netherlands, alongside the EU, Germany, and Greece, has joined the US-led Pax Silica AI initiative. X-FAB in Germany received €127.4 million from the CHIPS ACT for its MEMS Foundry in Erfurt, supporting technological sovereignty. Europe is pushing back on Washington’s chip war, and some perceive Europe’s digital sovereignty era as potentially ended before it began.

**Americas:**
Qualcomm unveiled its Dragonfly lineup data center chip portfolio and a multi-generation CPU agreement with Meta, strategically aiming to diversify beyond its shrinking smartphone business and challenge Nvidia’s dominance, while also courting Chinese demand. Qualcomm's stock jumped 14% following these updates and its acquisition of inference software startup Modular Inc. Cerebras Systems' stock fell below its IPO price after disappointing earnings guidance. Micron Technology quadrupled its revenue growth in the most recent quarter, benefiting from surging demand linked to the artificial intelligence industry, and reported a gross margin jump to 84.9% from 39% a year ago. Teledyne MEMS expanded its manufacturing operations in Edmonton, Alberta, with support from the Government of Alberta, reinforcing the province’s role in the global semiconductor supply chain. The US is fueling a $50 million Texas chips expansion to quadruple indium phosphide wafer production. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) partnered with Amkor to accelerate advanced packaging in the US. President Donald Trump confirmed a deal for Intel to make chips for Apple in the US, marking a significant win for US manufacturing. Nokia announced a major expansion of its US semiconductor advanced test and packaging operations in Pennsylvania to bolster AI growth. Quantum Computing Inc. acquired NHanced Semiconductors. Brewer Science, based in the US, acquired Heraeus Epurio’s chemicals unit.

</EXEC>
<LITHO>
**Asia:**
Micron Technology expects early product shipments from its Taiwan fab site by mid-2027, which could enhance its competitive edge in the memory market. IMEC has demonstrated two advances in ferroelectric memory research, potentially enabling next-generation RAM and NAND replacements.

**Europe:**
ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet confirmed that China can currently purchase older-generation deep ultraviolet (DUV) tools, which were first shipped about a decade ago, noting that the proposed US MATCH Act would put these off limits. ASML denied selling EUV chipmaking tools to China amidst US concerns. The Netherlands, a key player with ASML, is part of the Pax Silica AI initiative, despite broader European pushback on Washington's chip war, which aims to secure the AI supply chain across chips, critical minerals, energy, and compute. ZEISS in Germany produces ultra-precise optics essential for ASML.

**Americas:**
The US is fueling a $50 million Texas chips expansion to quadruple indium phosphide wafer production.
</LITHO>
<REE>
**Asia:**
China tightened export controls on indium amid rising AI demand. The G7 critical minerals push targets AI and chip supply chain risk. China also implemented export controls targeting US rare earth and other firms.

**Africa:**
The U.S.-Congo Cobalt Deal puts new pressure on China’s minerals empire, with the Department of War and Department of Energy announcing plans to bolster the critical minerals supply chain. President Tinubu of Nigeria demanded an end to African resource exploitation, urging industrialization and value addition to combat poverty. Zambia and the US expanded the scope of a $491 million agricultural grant to strengthen the critical minerals supply chain. Zimbabwe is scrutinizing Chinese lithium mining, and Africa’s top lithium producers face refinery bottlenecks and seek more time before an export ban. The G7’s $64 billion critical minerals push aims to open new opportunities for Africa, with a rare earth processing plant taking shape in West Africa.

**Europe:**
Japan and France are moving to reduce their reliance on Chinese heavy rare earths by backing a recycling project in southwestern France. This project is expected to supply materials used in high-performance permanent magnets for electric vehicles, defense equipment, and aerospace.

**Americas:**
The U.S.-Congo Cobalt Deal aims to put pressure on China’s minerals empire, with the Department of War and Department of Energy planning to bolster the critical minerals supply chain. President Donald Trump has secured a major win against China in the African rare earth minerals race.
</REE>

China's premier urged AI governance to avoid "losing control." The China International Supply Chain Expo debuted an AI section, with a focus on AI applications. Alibaba is suing the US Defense Department to remove its "Chinese military company" designation. Japan reported worsening difficulties in procuring naphtha and other oil products for nearly 70% of surveyed firms in May. South Korea's IPO activity has lagged compared to regional peers.

**Europe:**
Dutch Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma visited Washington to oppose the MATCH Act. The EU, Germany, the Netherlands, and Greece have joined the US-led Pax Silica AI initiative. Europe is pushing back on Washington’s chip war, and some perceive Europe’s digital sovereignty era as potentially having ended before it began.

**Americas:**
President Donald Trump had a testy meeting with Republican senators where he told Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy to sit down after questions arose about the War Powers Resolution. President Trump expressed feeling "let down" by NATO members for not meeting defense spending targets during an Oval Office meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

**Oceania:**

</GEO>
<MILITARY>
**Americas:**
The U.S. Army established the Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) common data layer baseline following operational validations at the 4th Infantry Division Ivy Sting-Ivy Mass series and the 25th Infantry Division Lightning Forge. Quantum computers present serious national security risks, particularly in breaking codes.

**Oceania:**
Australia signed a $2.5 billion deal with Canada to export radar technology, boosting the North American nation’s surveillance capabilities.
</MILITARY>
<CONCLUSION>The global technological and resource landscape is characterized by intensifying strategic competition, with AI development and critical mineral supply chains at the core. The United States is actively working to onshore and secure its semiconductor and mineral supply chains, while encountering pushback from European allies regarding restrictive trade measures like the MATCH Act. China is heavily investing in its domestic chip industry and leveraging its control over critical minerals as geopolitical tools. These actions by major powers are driving diversification efforts in regions like Africa and stimulating localized manufacturing initiatives across Europe and the Americas. The dual-use nature of advanced technologies like AI and quantum computing introduces significant national security considerations, prompting military advancements in command and control while highlighting vulnerabilities related to code-breaking capabilities. The intersection of economic competition, technological advancement, and resource control defines the current geopolitical environment.</CONCLUSION>

<INDIA>India is actively seeking semiconductor investments and multilateral funding at the Pax Silica summit in Washington D.C., aiming to leverage the US's $250 million seed fund to bolster its growing semiconductor manufacturing and design capabilities. Kinaxis is strengthening its presence in India as enterprises adopt AI for supply chain resilience. India is emerging as a key market for Everpure in the Asia Pacific Japan (APJ) region, driven by AI-led data center investments and modern storage solutions. India's AI boom faces a critical water crunch, as data centers, crucial for AI infrastructure, consume vast amounts of water, impacting cities like Hyderabad and Bengaluru, which already face shortages. A fire at STT Global Data Centres disrupted Google Cloud operations across India, exposing vulnerabilities in India's digital infrastructure and highlighting risks of data centralization and third-party dependencies. Indian onion exporters are urging the government against imposing export curbs, citing a surge in wholesale prices at Lasalgaon market due to delayed sowing and adverse weather impacting production. India's ambitious industrial expansion, targeting a 25% GDP contribution from manufacturing, faces a critical hurdle due to water scarcity, necessitating a focus on water resilience for companies. India and Iran are exploring opportunities to cooperate in the energy sector, as stated by Minister Puri.</INDIA>

<WEST_ASIA>The Israeli military has surrounded an underground base in southern Lebanon, where dozens of Hezbollah militants are reportedly trapped under the village of Tebnit. Israel plans to implement AI to teach English to middle schoolers to address massive teacher shortages. Israel needs to strengthen cybersecurity enforcement as AI accelerates attacks. Following missile strikes, an Israeli team developed a rapid AI building-map tool. Israel aims to become an AI superpower, with an estimated price tag of tens of billions of dollars. Publicis Israel has entered the AI arena with a data, media, and creative system. The UAE has introduced an AI-generated spokesperson for international outreach and created a dedicated artificial intelligence and data authority to build a "government of the future." 38% of UAE and Saudi firms have agentic AI in production, which is the highest globally. Visa launched AI-driven everyday cashback in the UAE with Mashreq and Rezolve AI. Saudi Arabia urged responsible AI governance at the UN. President Donald Trump had a testy meeting with Republican senators, telling Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy to sit down after questions arose about the War Powers Resolution. President Trump became frustrated with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu during negotiations for a peace deal with Hamas, remarking, "The Jews are sick of you." President Trump also complained to NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte that NATO members had not met defense spending targets. A $30 billion cancer breakthrough is under threat from Iran turmoil. Iran has reportedly agreed to nuclear inspections, a development affirmed by Vance, aligning with previous agreements. The IAEA chief indicated that inspectors would visit nuclear sites under an Iran-U.S. interim deal. The US energy secretary stated that the US has ended Iran's ability to close the Strait of Hormuz and projected that Iran would return to exporting similar oil volumes as during the Biden era. Oil prices touched pre-war levels on rising Middle East supply, though inflation accelerated in May due to the Iran war. The US and Iran are considering extending their ceasefire by two weeks. Egypt and Iran are facing a crucial World Cup game in the shadow of geopolitics.</WEST_ASIA>

<FINAL_CONCLUSION>The coming period will likely see continued intensification of the US-China tech rivalry, particularly in AI chips and critical minerals, with an emphasis on supply chain resilience and diversification among allied nations. European nations, while participating in initiatives like Pax Silica, will also continue to assert their own interests regarding export controls. The increasing demand for AI infrastructure will exacerbate energy and water resource constraints, as exemplified by India's challenges, necessitating innovative solutions and potentially driving new geopolitical flashpoints. In West Asia, the delicate balance of energy markets, security dynamics, and AI integration will remain a significant focus, with the implications of ongoing negotiations and military postures continuously influencing regional stability. The strategic importance of critical minerals will escalate, prompting further international cooperation and competition to secure access and processing capabilities. Advancements in quantum computing will introduce new dimensions to national security, requiring proactive measures in encryption and defense.</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
